project_overview.purpose: A Spring Boot REST API for the Sakila database, covering catalog, customer, location, payment, rental, staff, store, and auth workflows.
functionality: Manages film and actor data, including their relationships and detail views.
Manages customers and their related payment and rental history views.
Manages addresses and cities as part of the location data model.
Manages payment records and payment detail views.
Manages rental lifecycle operations, including return processing.
Manages staff records and staff detail views.
Provides a login endpoint that issues JWT-based authentication tokens.
Exposes sales report views by category and by store.
Wraps many read models in HATEOAS response representations.
Generates OpenAPI and Postman artifacts from REST Docs tests.
Exposes actuator and Prometheus monitoring endpoints.
project_overview.architecture: The application is organized as a layered Spring Boot service. HTTP requests enter controller classes under the configured `/api/v1` context path, then flow into domain services and repository/query layers for persistence and custom projections. Many read operations are mapped into DTOs and then wrapped in Spring HATEOAS representation models before being returned. Cross-cutting infrastructure is configured separately for security, JWT, JPA, Redis, Querydsl/Blaze-Persistence, logging, and documentation generation.

cross_cutting_concerns.name: Security
cross_cutting_concerns.description: Uses Spring Security with JWT support and password encoding to protect the REST API and handle login flows.

cross_cutting_concerns.name: Persistence
cross_cutting_concerns.description: Uses JPA, MySQL, Querydsl, and Blaze-Persistence for entity mapping, repository access, and custom query projections.

cross_cutting_concerns.name: API representation
cross_cutting_concerns.description: Uses DTOs and Spring HATEOAS assemblers/representation models to shape API responses.

cross_cutting_concerns.name: Observability
cross_cutting_concerns.description: Exposes actuator and Prometheus endpoints and configures logging-related infrastructure.

cross_cutting_concerns.name: Documentation generation
cross_cutting_concerns.description: Builds REST Docs-based reference material, OpenAPI output, and a Postman collection during the build.

findings.title: Generic codes share server-error status
findings.detail: Both generic entries map to HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR on lines 10-11. That may be intentional, but it means the WARN variant is still represented as an HTTP 500 rather than a non-error status or a different client-facing code.

findings.title: Private fields appear to exist for field-name generation
findings.detail: The class is private-constructor only and the fields on lines 11-50 are not assigned or read in this file. This strongly suggests they exist to drive Lombok's field-name constant generation rather than to store runtime state, which is a maintainability detail worth noting.

findings.title: Null lookup can throw on unknown ids
findings.detail: The method parses the trailing digits and immediately dereferences the lookup result at line 146. If the suffix does not match any enum id, `ID_MAP.get(...)` returns null and `country.getCountry()` will throw a NullPointerException. There is no fallback for unknown ids.

findings.title: Null input is not handled
findings.detail: `replaceCountryIdToCountryInString` calls `matcher.find()` on the provided argument without a null check at lines 142-143. Passing null will fail before any replacement logic runs.

findings.title: Country name constants do not fully match enum labels
findings.detail: Several enum entries use display names from `Constants`, but some constants differ from the enum name or common spelling, such as `KAZAKHSTAN` being "Kazakstan" at line 203 and `REUNION` being "Réunion" at line 231. This can affect string-based lookups and any code expecting consistent country labels.

findings.title: Inconsistent country spelling in constants
findings.detail: Some literals use spellings that differ from the enum identifiers or common English forms, such as `KAZAKHSTAN = "Kazakstan"` at line 203 and `REUNION = "Réunion"` at line 231. This is fine if intentional, but it is noteworthy because these strings are used for lookup and output formatting.

findings.title: Factory returns base type, not DTO subtype
findings.detail: Although the class extends ProblemDetail, the factory method instantiates and returns ProblemDetail directly. That makes the subclass itself effectively unused and may confuse callers expecting an ErrorResponseDto instance.

findings.title: No null check on errorCode
findings.detail: The factory dereferences errorCode immediately to read status and phrase. If a null value is passed, it will fail with a NullPointerException rather than a controlled error response.

findings.title: Page-to-list mapping drops pagination
findings.detail: The `mapToDtoList(Page<T>)` contract returns only `List<U>` on line 14, so any pagination metadata from the source page is not preserved in the result. That may be intentional, but callers cannot recover page information from this API.

findings.title: Schema/visitor metadata conflicts with output
findings.detail: `getSchema` reports `empty_string` while `acceptJsonFormatVisitor` advertises `expectNullFormat`, but both serialization methods actually write an empty string. The mixed metadata may confuse tooling or consumers that rely on Jackson introspection rather than observed output.

findings.title: Type information is ignored
findings.detail: `serializeWithType` discards `typeSer` and writes a plain string at lines 37-40. If this serializer is used in a context where polymorphic type ids are expected, those ids will not be emitted.

findings.title: Stack traces are printed directly
findings.detail: The handlers call e.printStackTrace() in addition to logging at lines 18, 26, and 34. This bypasses the logging framework and can produce duplicated or inconsistent error output in production logs.

findings.title: Repeated exception-to-response pattern
findings.detail: All three handlers follow the same logging and response-building pattern at lines 14-20, 22-28, and 30-36. This duplication makes it harder to keep error handling behavior consistent if the response format changes.

findings.title: Unconditional request cast
findings.detail: Line 14 casts the generic `ServletRequest` to `HttpServletRequest` without checking the actual request type. If this filter is applied outside an HTTP servlet context, it will fail with a `ClassCastException` before any logging context is set.

findings.title: Header value is used without normalization
findings.detail: Line 15 copies the incoming `X-Request-ID` header directly into MDC when present. The code does not trim or validate the header value, so empty or malformed identifiers can be propagated into logs.

findings.title: Authentication failures are not handled
findings.detail: The filter calls authenticationManager.authenticate(token) directly at line 27 and does not catch AuthenticationException or other runtime failures. An invalid or malformed token will therefore abort the request before line 30 instead of being treated as an unauthenticated request.

findings.title: Login bypass is path-exact only
findings.detail: The filter excludes only requests whose servlet path equals "/login" at line 35. Other login-related paths or context-path variations will still be filtered, which may be too narrow for the intended endpoint coverage.

findings.title: Token decoding errors are not handled
findings.detail: The provider calls jwtTokenProvider.decodeToken(accessToken) at line 23 and does not catch exceptions from decoding or parsing. A malformed or tampered token can therefore fail authentication with an unchecked exception instead of a clean authentication rejection.

findings.title: Authorities claim is assumed to be present
findings.detail: The code iterates over authorities immediately after reading the claim at lines 29-31, but it never checks for null. If the claim is missing, authentication will fail with a NullPointerException.

findings.title: Supports only the exact token class
findings.detail: supports() uses equals() at line 40, so subclasses or proxy types of JwtAuthenticationToken will not be recognized. That is stricter than necessary for many Spring Security configurations.

findings.title: Created tokens have no expiration
findings.detail: createToken() sets only the issued-at timestamp at lines 35-39 and never adds an expiration claim. That means issued tokens do not naturally expire, which weakens revocation and session-lifetime control.

findings.title: Token parsing can throw unchecked exceptions
findings.detail: decodeToken() directly parses the token at line 46 without handling malformed, expired, or signature-invalid JWTs. Callers must be prepared for runtime failures when decoding user-supplied tokens.

findings.title: Uses null to mean no filter
findings.detail: The helper methods intentionally return null when a condition or value is absent (lines 10, 14, 41). This is a common Querydsl pattern, but it requires every caller to handle null-safe predicate composition correctly.

findings.title: Range bounds are inclusive only
findings.detail: The range helper uses between, goe, and loe (lines 35, 37, 39), so all generated comparisons are inclusive. If callers need exclusive bounds, this utility does not provide them.

findings.title: Logs request headers and payloads
findings.detail: The filter is configured to include headers and request payloads in logs at lines 21-25. That can expose secrets, tokens, and personal data if sensitive requests reach this logger.

findings.title: Uses default Jackson typing for cache values
findings.detail: The cache serializer activates default typing for non-final types at lines 42-45. Polymorphic typing broadens what Jackson will deserialize from Redis values, so the safety of this choice depends on strict control of cached data.

findings.title: RedisTemplate uses unspecified serializers
findings.detail: The RedisTemplate is created and only given a connection factory at lines 34-36. No key or value serializers are configured here, so its serialization behavior is left to framework defaults and is not aligned in code with the explicit cache serializer setup below.

findings.title: Disables CORS at the security layer
findings.detail: The filter chain disables CORS at line 26. If cross-origin requests are expected, this configuration prevents security-layer CORS handling and must be matched by some other explicit arrangement; otherwise browser clients may be blocked.

findings.title: No request-body validation
findings.detail: The method consumes `AuthorityDto.Login` directly from the body and immediately dereferences `login.getEmail()` and `login.getPassword()` without any visible null or field validation on lines 24-26. If the payload is missing or incomplete, this can fail before any controlled error handling occurs.

findings.title: Login response carries no body
findings.detail: On lines 29-31 the endpoint returns only headers with an empty body. That is acceptable if the API contract is intentional, but the code does not document whether clients should read the token from the `Authorization` header or expect another response shape.

findings.title: Token is returned in response header only
findings.detail: The JWT is exposed through `headers.setBearerAuth(jwt)` on line 30. This is a deliberate pattern, but it means clients and intermediaries must be prepared to handle bearer tokens in headers rather than a body field; the code shown does not add any cache-control or related response hardening.

findings.title: Empty database string will fail to parse
findings.detail: `convertToEntityAttribute` splits the input on commas and immediately passes each token to `UserRole.valueOf` (lines 28-30). If `dbData` is an empty string, `split(",")` yields a single empty token, which will not match any enum constant and will throw at runtime.

findings.title: Null inputs are rejected with generic exceptions
findings.detail: Both conversion methods throw a bare `IllegalArgumentException` when their input is null (lines 15-17 and 25-27). This makes the failure mode explicit, but there is no message to help diagnose which value was null.

findings.title: Parsing logic assumes exact enum names
findings.detail: The entity conversion uses `UserRole.valueOf` directly on each stored token (lines 28-30). This ties the database format to the enum constant names and provides no accommodation for case differences or legacy values.

findings.title: JPA converter annotation on DTO fields
findings.detail: The nested DTOs annotate `authority` with `@Convert(converter = UserRoleConverter.class)` on lines 36-37 and 69-71. `@Convert` is a persistence-mapping concern, so placing it on DTOs suggests mixing transport and persistence concerns and may have no effect when these objects are only used as request/response models.

findings.title: Password is not validated
findings.detail: `password` is exposed in all three DTO shapes, but only `email` has bean-validation constraints. The code does not enforce presence or length for passwords on lines 32-33, 66-67, and 97-98, so invalid or empty passwords can pass validation unless checked elsewhere.

findings.title: Null identifiers compare equal
findings.detail: `equals` and `hashCode` use only `authorityId` on lines 39-50. Because `Objects.equal(null, null)` is true, two newly created instances with a null `authorityId` will compare equal and share the same hash code, which can be surprising in collections.

findings.title: Null emails compare equal
findings.detail: `equals` and `hashCode` depend only on `email` on lines 73-84. Instances with a null email will compare equal, which can be problematic if this DTO is created before validation or used in hash-based collections.

findings.title: Equality includes mutable entity state
findings.detail: The `equals`/`hashCode` implementation uses `authorityId`, `email`, and `authority` (lines 50-63). Because `email` and `authority` are mutable persistent fields, changing them after an entity is used in hashed collections can break lookups and equality consistency.

findings.title: Entity identity is mixed with business fields
findings.detail: `equals` compares both the generated identifier and domain fields (lines 51-58), which can make equality depend on persistence state as well as current field values. That design can be surprising for JPA entities and may not match identity semantics expected elsewhere in the application.

findings.title: Constants nested inside enum
findings.detail: The enum embeds a separate `Constants` holder for the same role names used by the enum values. This duplicates the canonical role strings in two places and can make future changes error-prone if one side is updated without the other.

findings.title: Public authority map is exposed directly
findings.detail: `AUTHORITY_MAP` is public and final, so callers can depend on this concrete reverse-lookup structure directly. That makes the enum API less flexible if the lookup strategy ever needs to change.

findings.title: String constants duplicate enum names
findings.detail: Each constant repeats the role identifier already present in the enclosing enum values. This duplication increases the chance of mismatches between the enum constant names and the string values they expose.

findings.title: Email lookup may return null
findings.detail: The custom finder on line 9 returns an entity directly rather than an Optional, so a missing email will be represented as null. Callers must handle that case explicitly to avoid null-related failures.

findings.title: Repository exposes a single-column lookup
findings.detail: The only custom query method is a direct email-based lookup on line 9. This is straightforward, but its behavior depends on email uniqueness, which is not visible in this file.

findings.title: Missing not-found handling
findings.detail: `loadUserByUsername` calls `authorityRepository.findAuthorityEntityByEmail(username)` and immediately dereferences the result at lines 22-27. If the repository returns `null` or an empty optional-like value, this can fail with a null-related exception instead of the expected `UsernameNotFoundException` declared by the method.

findings.title: Password check accepts null inputs implicitly
findings.detail: `findUser` forwards both `email` and `password` directly into lookup and `passwordEncoder.matches(...)` without any explicit validation at lines 31-34. A null or blank value may trigger unexpected exceptions or ambiguous authentication failures.

findings.title: Unused password encoder in user-loading path
findings.detail: The service injects `PasswordEncoder` at line 17, but it is only used in `findUser` and not in the `UserDetailsService` contract method. This suggests the class mixes authentication lookup and credential verification responsibilities in one component.

findings.title: No input validation before token creation
findings.detail: `authenticateToken` uses `user` and `jwt` directly at lines 14-16 without checking for null or blank values. Invalid inputs can produce runtime failures or delegate malformed credentials into the authentication manager.

findings.title: Thin delegation to authentication manager
findings.detail: The method is a small adapter that converts domain inputs into a Spring Security authentication token and delegates the actual verification to `AuthenticationManager` at lines 15-16. This keeps the service focused, but the method itself exposes no success/failure contract beyond thrown exceptions.

findings.title: Wrong type passed to superclass constructor
findings.detail: The constructor at line 18 passes `FilmDetailsDto.FilmDetails.class` as the first argument to `RepresentationModelAssemblerSupport`, while the other assemblers pass a controller class. That first argument is used to resolve link-building context, so this looks like a likely copy/paste error and may break link generation or assembler behavior.

findings.title: Raw filter parsing can fail at runtime
findings.detail: The film-list endpoint converts request parameters directly with `Year.parse(releaseYear)` and `FilmRating.valueOf(rating)` and looks up the category via a lowercased map key. Invalid or unexpected values will throw parsing exceptions instead of returning a controlled client error. The same applies to `Integer.valueOf(...)` in the add-film endpoint when the map entry is missing or not numeric.

findings.title: Generic request maps are not validated
findings.detail: The add-film and search endpoints accept `Map<String, String>` bodies and immediately read keys like `filmId` and `name` without checking presence or format. Missing keys produce null lookups, and malformed numeric input will fail before the service layer can handle it.

findings.title: No explicit request-body validation
findings.detail: The controller methods that accept request bodies (`addActor`, `updateActor`, `addActorFilm`, and `searchActorByName`) do not show any bean validation or manual checks. findings.title: Update result is computed but unused

findings.title: Query parameter parsing can fail
findings.detail: The listing endpoint converts `releaseYear` with `Year.parse` and `rating` with `FilmRating.valueOf` without guarding against invalid input. Bad values will raise runtime exceptions instead of being handled explicitly at the controller boundary.

findings.title: Unknown category values are silently ignored
findings.detail: The category filter uses a lookup map and passes the result directly into the filter object. If the incoming category does not match a known key, the value becomes null and the request is treated as if no category filter was supplied.

findings.title: Update result is discarded

findings.title: Null database values are rejected

findings.title: Unknown category ids map to null

findings.title: Null database values are rejected

findings.detail: The nested payload uses JPA @Convert on fields at lines 54-55 and 73-74, even though this type is a DTO. That coupling can make the model harder to reuse and suggests persistence concerns are leaking into the API layer.

findings.title: DTO container with multiple nested shapes
findings.detail: The type groups several distinct DTO roles into one outer class, which centralizes naming but also mixes API response, request, and persistence-style row models in a single file. This is intentional in the shown code, but it increases coupling between unrelated payload shapes.

findings.title: Ignored fields still carry JSON names

findings.title: Ignored relation fields still named as JSON properties

findings.title: Ignored relation fields still annotated as JSON

findings.title: Update method accepts null input unchecked

findings.title: Id fields are marked non-insertable and non-updatable

findings.detail: All payment DTO variants are defined as nested static classes in one outer type, which keeps them grouped but also makes the file larger and couples unrelated payload shapes to the same source file.

findings.title: Ignored associations still carry JSON names
findings.detail: The association fields are annotated with both JsonIgnore and JsonProperty on lines 50-63. Because they are ignored for JSON, the JsonProperty names do not contribute to the JSON payload, which can be confusing for readers and may suggest a serialized shape that the code does not actually expose.

findings.title: No field validation on request payload
findings.detail: The request DTO declares several business-critical fields on lines 97-110, but there are no validation annotations or constraints shown. As written, null values or invalid amounts/dates are not rejected by this type itself.

findings.title: Response flattens wrapped payment payload
findings.detail: The payment field is annotated with JsonUnwrapped on lines 141-142, so the response serializes the nested Payment directly into the response body. This is a deliberate shape choice that should be kept consistent with clients expecting a flattened contract.

findings.title: Update leaves associations stale
findings.detail: The update method assigns only the foreign-key fields at lines 91-96 and does not synchronize the related object references declared at lines 72-87. After calling update, the entity can have mismatched scalar IDs and association fields until they are refreshed separately.

findings.title: Last-update field is overwritten manually
findings.detail: The update method copies lastUpdate from the source entity at line 96 even though the field is also annotated with @UpdateTimestamp at lines 67-70. This mixes automatic timestamp management with manual assignment and can make the effective update time depend on the caller.

findings.title: Update method accepts null source fields
findings.detail: The method performs direct assignments from the input entity without any null checks or invariants at lines 91-96. If callers pass an entity with missing required values, those nulls will be copied into this instance.

findings.title: Unimplemented repository methods return no data
findings.detail: `findAllPaymentDetailsList()` returns `null` and `findPaymentDetailsById()` returns `Optional.empty()` on lines 35-43, so any caller expecting payment details will always receive no result. This is a functional gap rather than a fallback implementation.

findings.title: Category aggregation groups only by category id
findings.detail: The category sales query selects `filmCategory.categoryId` but groups only by that id on lines 55-64. If different category entities can share the same id representation or if the projection needs more category attributes, the query may not fully define the projected data; the code shown does not indicate whether the selected field is sufficient for the DTO.

findings.title: Store aggregation groups only by store id
findings.detail: The store sales query groups by `store.storeId` on lines 78-93 while projecting city, country, and manager fields derived from joined tables. The code assumes those joined values are uniquely determined by store id; if that assumption changes, the projection could become ambiguous.

findings.title: Result mutation after fetch
findings.detail: `calculateSalesByStore()` fetches DTOs and then mutates each result in a post-processing loop on lines 94-96. This creates a two-step projection that is harder to reason about than building the final value directly in the query.

findings.title: Optional return with exception on empty
findings.detail: `getPaymentDetails` returns `Optional<PaymentDto.Payment>` but throws `ResourceNotFoundException` when the repository returns empty, so callers never receive an empty Optional from this path. This makes the return type misleading and the API harder to use consistently.

findings.title: Create uses request rental id, not rental argument
findings.detail: `createPayment` accepts a `RentalDto.Rental rental` argument but sets `.rentalId(model.getRentalId())` while separately wiring `.rentalByRentalId(rental)`. If the request and supplied rental disagree, the stored object can contain inconsistent rental references.

findings.title: Delete has no explicit missing-record handling
findings.detail: `deletePayment` delegates directly to `paymentRepository.deleteById(paymentId)` without checking whether the payment exists or translating failures. If the id is missing, any repository exception will propagate as-is.

findings.title: Self link depends on non-null rental id
findings.detail: The self link is built from `entity.getRentalId()` on line 26 without any null check. If a rental without an id reaches this method, link generation may fail or produce an invalid link.

findings.title: Assembler is tightly coupled to controller methods
findings.detail: The assembler constructs links by calling `RentalController` methods directly on lines 26-29. This keeps the links in sync with controller signatures, but it also couples the assembler to that controller API.

findings.title: Request bodies are not validated
findings.detail: The controller accepts create, update, and return inputs directly and only applies ad hoc defaults for missing dates. There is no visible validation or error handling for required ids or malformed values before calling the service, so invalid requests may fail later or produce unclear errors.

findings.title: String map payload is weakly typed
findings.detail: The return endpoint accepts a generic Map<String, String> and looks up the "returnDate" key by name. This makes the contract fragile and easy to misuse, because missing or misspelled keys are only discovered at runtime.

findings.title: Unused service results
findings.detail: Both updateRental and returnDvd store the service return value in a local variable but never use it in the response. This adds noise and suggests the controller is discarding information that might otherwise be returned to the client.

findings.title: Controller mutates incoming request objects
findings.detail: The create and return endpoints modify the submitted request data in place to inject the current timestamp. That couples HTTP handling to defaulting behavior and can make request handling harder to reason about or reuse.

findings.title: Single file groups multiple DTO variants
findings.detail: This type bundles read models, create/update requests, a return-specific request, and a response wrapper in one outer class (lines 19-222). That keeps the related transfer shapes together, but also makes the file carry several distinct API contracts at once.

findings.title: Linked objects are ignored in JSON
findings.detail: The relation fields are annotated with both `@JsonIgnore` and `@JsonProperty` (lines 49-62). As written, the DTO keeps these references out of the serialized JSON while still naming them, which is intentional in many designs but can be confusing to maintainers.

findings.title: Equality omits navigation properties
findings.detail: `equals` and `hashCode` use only the scalar rental fields (lines 64-82) and ignore the linked inventory, customer, and staff objects. That is fine if these references are purely derived, but two instances with different loaded relations will still compare equal.

findings.title: No field validation is present
findings.detail: The request type exposes nullable fields for all inputs and contains no validation annotations or checks on lines 96-109. Invalid or incomplete creation data would therefore need to be rejected elsewhere, if at all.

findings.title: No validation on update fields
findings.detail: The update request declares all fields as optional nullable values without any validation constraints or guard logic (lines 140-153). If partial or malformed updates are not intended, that enforcement must happen outside this DTO.

findings.title: Return request has no validation
findings.detail: The return request accepts three nullable fields and contains no validation annotations or checks (lines 184-191). This leaves required-input enforcement to surrounding layers.

findings.title: Response unwraps the nested rental
findings.detail: The response embeds the rental object with `@JsonUnwrapped` (lines 205-206), so the rental fields are flattened into the response payload. This is a deliberate API shape choice, but it means the wrapper contributes no separate JSON namespace for the rental content.

findings.title: Null rental wrapper may serialize poorly
findings.detail: The response type allows the wrapped `rental` field to be absent because there is no validation or constructor enforcement on lines 205-206. If code creates the response without setting `rental`, consumers may receive an incomplete payload.

findings.title: Update copies foreign-key ids but not associations
findings.detail: The update method assigns the id fields for inventory, customer, and staff at lines 95-98, but it leaves the corresponding @ManyToOne references unchanged. That can create an in-memory mismatch between the scalar foreign-key values and the associated entity objects after a merge-style update.

findings.title: Equality includes mutable timestamp fields
findings.detail: equals and hashCode include lastUpdate, and update also copies it from the source object. Because this field is expected to change on persistence updates, using it in equality can make entity identity unstable across updates and persistence lifecycle changes.

findings.title: No null guard in update method
findings.detail: The method dereferences the input entity directly at lines 94-99 without checking for null. Passing null would throw a NullPointerException.

findings.title: Relationship fields are intentionally not mapped
findings.detail: The mapper ignores the nested inventory, customer, and staff associations when converting to DTOs and when mapping update requests to entities (lines 17-19, 30-32). This means those linked objects must be populated elsewhere if callers expect them to be present.

findings.title: Update timestamp set during mapping
findings.detail: Both entity-producing mappings set `lastUpdate` with `LocalDateTime.now()` (lines 25-26, 29-33, 37-38). This centralizes timestamp assignment in the mapper, but it also means the current time is taken at mapping time rather than by the persistence layer.

findings.title: Multiple entity mapping variants overlap
findings.detail: The interface defines several similar DTO-to-entity mappings with slightly different field handling (`mapToEntity`, `mapToEntity` for update requests, and `mapToRentEntity`) on lines 22-38. That overlap can make it harder to see which conversion path should be used for a given use case.

findings.title: Multiple matches resolved arbitrarily
findings.detail: The query applies only equality filters and then uses fetchFirst() without any explicit ordering. If more than one active rental matches the same customer and inventory pair, the returned row is unspecified from the code shown.

findings.title: Null arguments not checked
findings.detail: The method accepts customerId and inventoryId directly and uses them in equality predicates with no validation or null handling. Passing null values may lead to unexpected query behavior or runtime issues depending on Querydsl/JPA handling.

findings.title: Method name suggests ID but returns entity
findings.detail: The method name findRentedDvdRentalId implies it returns a rental identifier, but the implementation returns a RentalEntity object. This mismatch can confuse callers and maintainers.

findings.title: Overdue methods return null
findings.detail: Both overdue rental methods are declared as read-only service operations, but this one returns null instead of a value or an exception. Callers will receive a null BigDecimal, which is likely unintended and can cause downstream failures.

findings.title: Unvalidated map parsing can fail
findings.detail: The return flow parses customerId, inventoryId, and returnDate directly from a String map without checking for missing keys or malformed values. A missing entry or bad format will throw runtime parsing exceptions before the service can report a domain-specific error.

findings.title: Payment result is ignored after rental save
findings.detail: The rental is saved first and then a payment is created, but the payment result is stored in a local variable and never used. If payment creation fails after the rental save, the method relies on transaction rollback behavior that is not explicit here, and the saved rental/payment coordination is unclear.

findings.title: Delete ignores missing rental state
findings.detail: The delete operation delegates directly to repository deletion by id without checking whether the rental exists first. Depending on repository behavior, callers may get no domain-specific not-found feedback.

findings.title: Unused update result
findings.detail: The update endpoint stores the service return value in a local variable but never uses it before returning 200 OK. This adds noise and may hide an expectation that the updated entity should be reflected in the response or used for validation.

findings.title: Create endpoint does not return resource body
findings.detail: The create endpoint returns only a Location header and no response body after adding staff. That may be acceptable, but clients needing the created representation must issue another request.

findings.title: DTO mixes persistence conversion annotation
findings.detail: The nested `StaffDetails` DTO field `country` is annotated with `@Convert(converter = CountryConverter.class)` on lines 68-70. That annotation is typically used on JPA-managed entities, so placing it on a DTO can confuse layering and suggests persistence concerns are leaking into the API model.

findings.title: Persistence converter on DTO field
findings.detail: The `country` property uses `@Convert(converter = CountryConverter.class)` on lines 68-70. This couples the DTO to a JPA converter, which is unusual for a transfer object and may make the model harder to reuse outside persistence-related flows.

findings.title: Only username is constrained
findings.detail: The request and base DTO validate `username` with a size constraint, but other fields such as `firstName`, `lastName`, `addressId`, `storeId`, and `authorityId` have no visible validation. That leaves required-field and range checks to other layers, if any.

findings.title: Commented-out picture field remains in equality code
findings.detail: Both nested DTOs contain commented-out `picture` fields, and the equality/hash code implementations still carry commented references to them. This can confuse maintenance because the active object state no longer matches the commented comparison logic.

findings.title: Hypermedia wrapper uses nested unwrapped payload
findings.detail: The response type wraps a `Staff` object and unpacks it into the JSON payload while also extending a HATEOAS representation model. This is a deliberate API-shaping pattern, but it means the response structure is split between the wrapper and the nested DTO.

findings.title: Nested relations are hidden from JSON
findings.detail: The linked `addressByAddressId`, `storeByStoreId`, and `authorityByAuthorityId` fields are marked with `@JsonIgnore` while also having JSON property names. As written, they are excluded from serialization, so consumers will only see the scalar identifiers, not the nested related objects.

findings.title: Username length is the only enforced constraint
findings.detail: `username` is constrained to a length between 1 and 16, but no other field here is validated. If this DTO is used for input binding, missing or malformed values for the remaining fields would not be rejected by this class.

findings.title: Equality includes all mutable state
findings.detail: `equals` and `hashCode` consider the entire set of scalar fields, including `lastUpdate` and `active`. If any of these values change after the object is used in hash-based collections, lookups can become inconsistent.

findings.title: Request lacks presence checks for names
findings.detail: `firstName` and `lastName` are exposed as request fields but have no visible constraints. If these values are required by the service layer, that requirement is not expressed in the DTO itself.

findings.title: Relation identifiers are unvalidated
findings.detail: The request accepts `addressId`, `storeId`, and `authorityId` without any visible null or range constraints. Invalid or missing foreign-key values would need to be handled elsewhere.

findings.title: Commented-out picture field persists in request model
findings.detail: The request class still contains commented `picture` field references in equality and hash code logic. This suggests the model changed over time, but the stale comments were not cleaned up.

findings.title: Response wrapper extends representation model
findings.detail: The type is a thin envelope over a nested `Staff` DTO and inherits hypermedia support from the framework model. This is a standard response-wrapping pattern, but the actual payload is entirely delegated to the nested object.

findings.title: Equality depends on superclass state
findings.detail: `equals` first delegates to `super.equals(o)` before comparing the nested `staff` field. That means link-related state inherited from the representation model participates in equality, which can make behavior less obvious to callers.

findings.title: Update copies read-only foreign-key fields
findings.detail: The method assigns addressId, storeId, and authorityId on lines 106, 108, and 111, but those columns are mapped as insertable = false and updatable = false on lines 44-45, 56-57, and 74-75. That means changing these fields here will not be written directly by JPA, so the method can leave the entity state out of sync with what will actually persist unless the association fields are also updated.

findings.title: Mutable fields included in equality
findings.detail: equals and hashCode include mutable fields such as fullName, active, username, authorityId, and lastUpdate on lines 120-136. Because these values can change after persistence, the object's hash-based behavior can change over time, which is risky if instances are used in collections or as cache keys.

findings.title: Related entities are always omitted
findings.detail: The DTO mapping explicitly ignores the address, store, and authority associations on lines 14-16, so callers will never receive those nested objects from this mapper. That is fine if the API intentionally exposes a flat staff view, but it also means the mapper cannot be used when relationship data is needed.

findings.title: Update timestamp is always overwritten
findings.detail: The request-to-entity mapping sets lastUpdate with LocalDateTime.now() on line 22. This ensures a fresh timestamp for every mapped request, but it also discards any timestamp value that may exist in the source object and couples mapping to the system clock.

findings.title: Optional.of can throw on missing staff
findings.detail: Line 33 wraps `query.fetchFirst()` with `Optional.of(...)`. If the query returns no row, `fetchFirst()` is null and this will throw a NullPointerException instead of returning `Optional.empty()`.

findings.title: Single-result lookup does not enforce uniqueness
findings.detail: Lines 32-33 use `fetchFirst()` for an id-based lookup. If the query matches more than one row, only the first is returned and duplicate data would be hidden rather than detected.

findings.title: Optional return is misleading
findings.detail: Both lookup methods declare Optional return types, but they never return an empty Optional. In getStaff, absence becomes a ResourceNotFoundException at lines 32-34; in getStaffDetails, absence also throws at lines 46-49. Callers cannot use the Optional to represent a missing record, so the signature does not match the actual behavior.

findings.title: No input validation on ids or payloads
findings.detail: The service methods accept staffId and request models directly and pass them to repository/mapper operations without any explicit null or range checks (for example lines 32-33, 46-48, 56-57, 63-66, and 72). If invalid values can reach this layer, the resulting failures will come from downstream components rather than from clear service-level validation.

findings.title: Delete operation has no existence check
findings.detail: removeStaff delegates straight to deleteById at lines 71-72. If the id does not exist, the behavior depends on the repository implementation and may surface as a data-access exception instead of the same not-found handling used by the read/update methods.

findings.title: Links are built with an unpaged list call
findings.detail: The collection link is created with PageRequest-independent input by calling `getStoreList(Pageable.unpaged())` on line 30. This clearly targets the store list endpoint, but it hardcodes an unpaged variant of that route, so the assembler always advertises the same navigation shape regardless of the caller context.

findings.title: Collection navigation uses an unpaged list link
findings.detail: The store-list link is constructed via `getStoreList(Pageable.unpaged())` on line 28. That makes the generated link independent of any pagination state and may not match clients expecting page-specific navigation.

findings.title: Endpoints are limited to a manage role
findings.detail: Both report endpoints are protected with the same role requirement on lines 26 and 33, which means only callers with that authority can access sales reports. That is appropriate if intentional, but it is a hard access gate worth noting because no broader read-only role is allowed here.

findings.title: PUT binding differs from create endpoint
findings.detail: The create endpoint binds the request body with @RequestBody, but updateStore binds with @ModelAttribute on lines 57-60. That means the update endpoint will not accept the same JSON-style payload as the create endpoint unless callers submit form/query parameters instead, which is an API inconsistency that can surprise clients.

findings.title: Entity converter used on DTO field
findings.detail: The category field is annotated with a JPA attribute converter at line 34. This is unusual for a DTO and only makes sense if the object is also reused in persistence-related mapping; otherwise the annotation has no effect during plain JSON serialization.

findings.title: DTO mixes payload and hypermedia concerns
findings.detail: This type extends a HATEOAS representation model while also embedding the business payload via an unwrapped field on lines 65 and 69-70. That is a valid API pattern, but it couples the response DTO to Spring HATEOAS infrastructure and makes the plain payload harder to reuse independently.

findings.title: Mutable fields used in hash code
findings.detail: The equality and hash code implementations include mutable fields such as filmId, storeId, and lastUpdate (lines 48-56). Because the class has setters, changing those fields after insertion into a hash-based collection can make the object unreachable in that collection.

findings.title: Nested DTO mixes identity and relations
findings.detail: The type stores both raw foreign key fields and object references for film and store (lines 21-41). This is workable, but it couples the DTO to both identifier and navigation-style data, which can make serialization and mapping behavior harder to reason about.

findings.title: Redundant Jackson annotations on nested references
findings.detail: The nested store entity marks `staffByManagerStaffId` and `addressByAddressId` with both `@JsonIgnore` and `@JsonProperty` on lines 39-47. Since `@JsonIgnore` suppresses Jackson serialization, the property name metadata is not used for JSON output and may confuse readers about the intended API shape.

findings.title: Mutable timestamp in equality and hash code
findings.detail: `lastUpdate` participates in both `equals` and `hashCode` on lines 54-63. If instances are placed in hash-based collections and the timestamp changes afterward, lookups and removals can become inconsistent.

findings.title: Ignored associations still declared as JSON properties
findings.detail: The related staff and address fields are annotated as ignored but also assigned JSON property names on lines 39-47. This makes the serialization intent harder to understand because the property names do not affect ignored output.

findings.title: Response model nests the actual payload
findings.detail: The response type wraps the store object inside a `RepresentationModel` and unwrapped field on lines 105-123. This is consistent with HATEOAS-style responses, but callers must know that the actual business data is nested in the `store` field rather than living directly on the response type.

findings.title: Equality includes all mutable fields
findings.detail: The custom equality and hash code are based on store, manager, and totalSales (lines 45-58). Because the fields are mutable via setters, instances used as map keys or set elements can become unstable if modified after insertion.

findings.title: Nested payload may be null
findings.detail: The response stores the sales payload in a single field with no visible validation or required-ness enforcement (lines 72-73). If callers build the object without setting it, serialization or downstream handling may see a null payload.

findings.title: Equality depends on superclass state
findings.detail: The custom equals implementation delegates to super.equals before comparing the nested sales object (lines 75-87). This makes equality depend on the RepresentationModel base state as well as the wrapped DTO, which is worth noting for objects used in collections or tests.

findings.title: Update method skips association references
findings.detail: The update implementation copies only filmId, storeId, and lastUpdate on lines 68-70, but leaves filmByFilmId and storeByStoreId unchanged. If this method is used to replace the entity state, the scalar foreign-key fields can no longer match the managed associations.

findings.title: Update method accepts null source
findings.detail: The method dereferences entity immediately on lines 68-70 without any null check. A null argument would throw a NullPointerException at runtime.

findings.title: Mapped foreign keys are read-only
findings.detail: The filmId and storeId columns are marked insertable=false and updatable=false on lines 36-44, so direct updates to these fields will not be written through JPA. The update method still assigns them on lines 68-69, which suggests the method may not have the intended persistence effect for these values.

findings.title: Update method skips association fields
findings.detail: The update method copies only the scalar foreign-key columns and timestamp at lines 69-71, but leaves staffByManagerStaffId and addressByAddressId unchanged. That can create an inconsistent in-memory entity where the FK values and the referenced objects no longer match.

findings.title: Update method accepts null source
findings.detail: The method dereferences entity directly at lines 69-71 without a null check. Passing null would throw a NullPointerException, so the caller must validate the argument beforehand.

findings.title: Timestamp set during mapping
findings.detail: The entity mapping assigns `lastUpdate` with `LocalDateTime.now()` directly in the mapper. This makes the mapping depend on the system clock and mixes a time-sensitive side effect into what is otherwise field translation.

findings.title: Optional.of may throw on missing result
findings.detail: `findStoreDetailsById` calls `query.fetchFirst()` and then immediately wraps the result with `Optional.of(...)` on line 45. If no row is found, `fetchFirst()` can return null, which would cause a `NullPointerException` instead of an empty `Optional`.

findings.title: Null result passed to DTO mutation
findings.detail: `findStoreDetailsById` calls `replaceCountryIdToCountry(result)` before checking whether a row was returned. When `fetchFirst()` yields null, line 44 will dereference a null DTO and fail.

findings.title: Staff lookup wraps nullable result with Optional.of
findings.detail: `findStoreStaffById` wraps `query.fetchFirst()` with `Optional.of(...)` on line 84. If the query returns no staff row, this will throw a `NullPointerException` instead of returning `Optional.empty()`.

findings.title: Store id is used without null guard
findings.detail: `findStoreStaff` always applies `where(store.storeId.eq(storeId))` on line 95. If `storeId` is null, the generated predicate may be invalid or unintended, and the method does not guard against that input.

findings.title: Single-result methods rely on fetchFirst without uniqueness guarantee
findings.detail: Both single-result methods use `fetchFirst()` on lines 43 and 84 even though the queries are not shown to enforce uniqueness beyond the filters. If multiple rows match, the code silently takes the first row rather than detecting ambiguity.

findings.title: Unimplemented staff association methods
findings.detail: The methods at lines 91-92 and 106-107 return null instead of performing any work. Any caller using these API paths will receive a null result, which is likely to cause downstream failures and means the advertised service operations are not implemented.

findings.title: Optional returned after throwing on miss
findings.detail: Methods such as getStore, getStoreDetails, and getStoreStaff throw a ResourceNotFoundException when nothing is found, yet still declare Optional return types and wrap/pass through the found value. That combination is misleading because the Optional does not represent absence here; it only ever contains a value on success.

findings.title: Delete does not verify existence
findings.detail: deleteStore calls repository.deleteById directly without first checking whether the store exists. Depending on repository behavior, the method may silently do nothing or surface a data-access exception rather than the service's not-found exception style used elsewhere.

findings.title: Auth model uses different identity rules across DTOs and entity
findings.detail: The domain defines identity inconsistently: the authority DTO compares by authorityId, the user DTO compares by email, and the JPA entity includes mutable state in equality. This makes it unclear which field is the stable identifier for auth records across controller, service, and persistence layers.

findings.title: Input and null handling is inconsistent across the catalog stack
findings.detail: Controllers parse filter parameters from raw request values, while service and repository methods dereference filter objects and identifiers without comprehensive guards. At the same time, the enum converters may return null for unknown database values, so invalid or missing inputs can surface as runtime failures or unexpected nulls instead of a consistent validation error path.

findings.title: Several custom repository extension points are declared but not implemented with behavior
findings.detail: The catalog module defines custom repository interfaces for category, film-actor, film-category, and film-text data access, but the corresponding implementation classes shown here are empty. That leaves the behavior of those extension points unknown in this code set and suggests the abstraction structure is broader than the implemented custom query logic currently visible.

findings.title: JWT failures are not normalized into the shared web error flow
findings.detail: JWT decoding and authentication are handled in the security layer, but the filter/provider path does not show explicit failure translation, while the MVC advice only covers web-layer exceptions. As a result, malformed or invalid bearer tokens may escape the standardized application error response path and surface as framework-level authentication failures instead of the common error payload.

findings.title: Shared helpers assume non-null inputs in several places
findings.detail: Multiple common components rely on callers to provide non-null values rather than enforcing a shared validation boundary. This is visible in the error-response factory, request-ID filter, country lookup helpers, and expression utilities, which all operate with minimal input guarding and can defer failures to runtime.

findings.title: Security and logging concerns are split across multiple config classes
findings.detail: Authentication, request logging, and HTTP security are configured in separate classes rather than a single security-focused module. This is workable, but it spreads closely related concerns across the configuration package and makes the full request-processing/security story harder to reason about from one place.

findings.title: Security filter config disables CORS at the security layer
findings.detail: The security setup explicitly turns off CORS handling, but no corresponding CORS configuration is visible in the supplied config summaries. Whether this is intentional or leaves cross-origin requests unsupported cannot be confirmed from the available code.

findings.title: Customer and filter inputs are passed through without consistent validation
findings.detail: The controller accepts customer ids and date/status query values without explicit validation, while the service/repository layers assume they are usable and parse or query them directly. This makes the input contract depend on runtime parsing and repository behavior rather than a consistent API-level validation rule.

findings.title: Paged collection links are built as unpaged links in both customer assemblers
findings.detail: Both response assemblers add collection links that point to the customer list without preserving pagination context. That means the hypermedia links do not reflect the paging model used by the list endpoint.

findings.title: Custom address lookup is unimplemented despite service/controller exposure
findings.detail: The location service and controller expose address list and detail flows, but the custom address repository implementation currently returns null for list retrieval and never finds an address by ID. That means the domain’s address projection/lookup path is not actually backed by data access code.

findings.title: Write requests are not validated at the controller boundary
findings.detail: The address and city request DTOs carry bean-validation constraints, but the controller summaries indicate that request bodies are not validated there. As a result, the domain defines validation rules that are not enforced where the HTTP requests enter the system.

findings.title: Delete handling differs from the read/update not-found behavior
findings.detail: The service layer translates missing records into not-found exceptions for selected read and update operations, but the delete paths do not perform that translation. This creates inconsistent API behavior across location operations when an identifier does not exist.

findings.title: Payment detail repository methods are exposed but not implemented
findings.detail: The custom repository interface exposes payment detail lookup operations, and the controller/service layer exposes a payment details endpoint, but the repository implementation leaves the lookup methods unimplemented and returns no data. This creates a gap between the public read surface and the backing data access layer.

findings.title: Delete flow has no cross-layer missing-record handling
findings.detail: The REST API exposes delete semantics for a payment, but the service implementation does not provide explicit handling for the case where the target payment is absent. That leaves deletion behavior dependent on lower layers rather than a domain-level response path.

findings.title: Overdue-rental contract is not implemented in the service
findings.detail: The service contract advertises overdue-rental calculation, but the implementation summary says the overdue methods return null. This means callers cannot rely on the published behavior of the rental service for overdue totals.

findings.title: Request handling relies on unvalidated input across controller and DTO layers
findings.detail: The controller accepts rental create/update/return payloads without validation, while the request DTOs also declare no field validation. This leaves the rental flow dependent on downstream parsing and service logic instead of rejecting invalid input at the boundary.

findings.title: Custom active-rental lookup can return an arbitrary match when multiple rows qualify
findings.detail: The custom repository searches for an active rental by customer and inventory and returns the first matching entity. If more than one row satisfies the lookup, the chosen result is not defined by the repository contract.

findings.title: Create endpoint returns no response body while response model support exists
findings.detail: The controller adds HATEOAS response modeling for staff resources, but the create flow only returns a location header and no body. That is inconsistent with the rest of the domain’s response-shaping approach and with the assembler support for wrapping created staff data.

findings.title: Request and service layers do not consistently enforce input constraints
findings.detail: The request DTO only constrains username length, while the service is documented as taking arbitrary ids and payloads without validation. This leaves names and foreign-key-style identifiers unchecked at the API boundary, despite the domain carrying multiple relational references.

findings.title: Single staff-detail lookup can fail on absent rows through Optional wrapping
findings.detail: The custom repository implementation wraps a single projected result in Optional.of, so a missing row would not be represented as an empty Optional. This conflicts with the surrounding repository/service contract that treats absent staff as a normal not-found case.

findings.title: Read and write models intentionally diverge, but some relation data is dropped in mapping
findings.detail: The mapper omits related entities when converting staff entities to DTOs, while the entity and DTOs both model address, store, and authority relationships. That means the API summary view cannot express those links even though they exist in persistence and in the DTO types.

findings.title: Update and delete flows are not symmetric in existence handling
findings.detail: The service translates missing records to a not-found exception for reads and updates, but delete has no existence check before removal. That makes delete behavior depend entirely on repository semantics rather than the domain’s explicit not-found handling.

findings.title: Representation concerns are duplicated across DTOs and assemblers
findings.detail: Several DTO types already embed HATEOAS response wrappers, and separate assemblers then add the navigation links for the same response shapes. This split is consistent across store details, store sales, and category sales, but it means payload and hypermedia concerns are distributed across multiple layers instead of being concentrated in one place.

findings.title: Store navigation links are built from unpaged collection endpoints
findings.detail: The store and store-details assemblers construct collection navigation links by pointing to the unpaged store-list endpoint. That keeps link generation simple, but the resulting navigation does not carry any pagination context because the target resource is a full list view.

findings.title: 11 boilerplate method(s) with cyclomatic complexity >= 11
findings.detail: Measured by lizard: FilmDetails.equals (CC 11), Film.equals (CC 16), FilmRequest.equals (CC 14), FilmEntity.equals (CC 16), CustomerDetails.equals (CC 12), CustomerEntity.equals (CC 11), Address.equals (CC 11), AddressEntity.equals (CC 11), StaffDetails.equals (CC 11), Staff.equals (CC 11), StaffEntity.equals (CC 11). These are hand-written equals/hashCode-style members classified as boilerplate, not business logic.

findings.title: README endpoint list differs from controller mappings
findings.detail: Controllers map /api/v1/location, /api/v1/login which the README does not list.

findings.title: README claims CRUD support; some listed resources lack HTTP verbs
findings.detail: Missing verbs per resource (from mappings): /api/v1/payments: POST; /api/v1/reports: DELETE, POST, PUT.
